questions.stem: A 27 year old woman who injects heroin has 8 days of fever, rigors, cough and pleuritic chest pain. There is a new pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge that is louder on inspiration. Her temperature is 39.1°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 104/66 mmHg and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. Chest X-ray (see item resources).

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Multiple cavitating nodules in both lungs: septic emboli.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Fever, IV drug use and a new right-sided murmur are tricuspid valve endocarditis, an emergency; vegetations embolise to the lungs giving multiple cavitating lesions.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.

clues: new pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge
steps.x: **IVDU + fever + new murmur** louder on inspiration (right-sided) = tricuspid IE, with **septic pulmonary emboli**.

elim: Aspiration causes right lower lobe consolidation and no new murmur.
Mitral IE gives an apical murmur louder on expiration and systemic emboli.
TB is subacute, upper zone, without a new murmur.
A pneumonia alone would not explain a new murmur louder on inspiration.

steps.x: **E. Tricuspid valve infective endocarditis.** IVDU + fever + new murmur = right-sided IE until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: A 35 year old man who injects drugs into his groin has 1 week of fever and a new pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge. Echocardiography shows a 14 mm vegetation on the tricuspid valve. His temperature is 38.8°C and pulse rate 112 bpm. Blood cultures are pending.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Tricuspid valve endocarditis in people who inject drugs is typically Staph. aureus from the skin, carried in the venous blood to the right heart first.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.
Skin organism injected into veins reaches the **right heart** first: **Staph. aureus**.

elim: Coxiella follows farm animal exposure.
Enterococci follow GI/GU procedures.
Strep. bovis is linked to colorectal cancer.
Strep. viridans follows dental disease, on left-sided abnormal valves.

steps.x: **C. Staphylococcus aureus.** IVDU tricuspid IE: Staph. aureus.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman with pulmonary hypertension has a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge. Her JVP is raised with large waves in systole and she has a tender, pulsatile liver edge. The examiner places the heel of his hand to the left of her sternum.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on palpation?
o: Heaving apex beat in the axilla
Tapping apex at the fifth intercostal space
questions.e: Tricuspid regurgitation with pulmonary hypertension and right ventricular overload causes a left parasternal heave, with prominent V waves and pulsatile hepatomegaly.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.

clues: pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge
steps.x: TR with an overloaded **right ventricle**: the RV lies behind the sternum, so feel a **parasternal heave**.

elim: A displaced tapping apex is not a sign of RV overload.
A heaving displaced apex is LV hypertrophy and dilatation.
A carotid thrill is aortic stenosis.
A tapping apex is mitral stenosis.

steps.x: **C. Left parasternal heave.** TR signs: V waves, parasternal heave, pulsatile liver.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man has breathlessness and ankle swelling. There is a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge. The examining doctor wants to show whether the murmur arises from the right side of the heart, using a simple bedside manoeuvre.
questions.q: Which manoeuvre would most likely make the murmur louder?
questions.e: Carvallo's sign: the tricuspid regurgitation murmur gets louder on inspiration because negative intrathoracic pressure increases venous return and flow across the right-sided valve.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.

clues: pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge
steps.x: Right-sided murmurs get louder with **inspiration** (more venous return to the right heart).

elim: Expiration accentuates left-sided murmurs.
Sitting forward in expiration is for aortic regurgitation.
Standing reduces venous return and softens most murmurs.
Valsalva reduces venous return and softens most murmurs.

steps.x: **B. Deep inspiration.** Carvallo's sign: TR louder on inspiration.

questions.stem: A 15 year old girl has breathlessness when running and fainted once during a cross-country race. There is an ejection systolic murmur loudest at the left second intercostal space, radiating to the left shoulder and louder on deep inspiration. It does not radiate to the carotids. Her JVP shows a large a wave.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Pulmonary stenosis presents in childhood with exertional syncope, an ejection systolic murmur in the pulmonary area radiating to the shoulder (not carotids), louder on inspiration, and a large a wave.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.

clues: fainted once during a cross-country race
does not radiate to the carotids
steps.x: Pulmonary area + shoulder (not carotids) + **louder on inspiration** + **large a wave** = PS.

elim: Aortic stenosis radiates to the carotids and is louder in expiration.
ASD gives fixed splitting of S2 and a flow murmur, without a large a wave.
HCM murmur is at the left sternal edge and gets louder on Valsalva and standing.
A VSD gives a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge.

steps.x: **D. Pulmonary stenosis.** Young, pulmonary area, radiates to shoulder, large a wave = pulmonary stenosis.

questions.stem: A 12 year old boy has moderate congenital pulmonary valve stenosis. He gets breathless on exertion. His pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 108/64 mmHg. The doctor examines his neck veins with him lying at 45°.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of the JVP?
questions.e: Pulmonary stenosis causes RV hypertrophy; the right atrium contracts hard against the stiff ventricle, giving a large a wave.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.
Obstructed RV outflow stiffens the RV; the RA squeezes harder: **large a wave**.

elim: An absent a wave is atrial fibrillation.
An absent y descent is tamponade.
Cannon a waves are complete heart block.
Giant v waves are tricuspid regurgitation.

steps.x: **E. Large a wave.** PS: large a wave in the JVP.

questions.stem: A 4 year old girl is referred with a heart murmur. She is short for her age with a broad webbed neck, widely spaced eyes, low-set ears and a pectus deformity. She has a normal female karyotype. There is an ejection systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border with a thrill.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying syndrome?
questions.e: Congenital pulmonary valve stenosis is associated with Noonan syndrome: short stature, webbed neck, low-set ears, pectus deformity and a normal karyotype.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.

clues: left upper sternal border with a thrill
steps.x: Turner-like features with a **normal karyotype** + **pulmonary stenosis** = **Noonan**.

elim: DiGeorge gives conotruncal defects with hypocalcaemia and immune deficiency.
Marfan gives tall stature, lens dislocation and aortic root dilatation.
Turner syndrome is 45,X and linked to coarctation and bicuspid aortic valve.
Williams gives supravalvular aortic stenosis and hypercalcaemia.

steps.x: **C. Noonan syndrome.** Pulmonary stenosis + Turner-like features + normal karyotype: Noonan syndrome.

questions.stem: A 7 year old boy with Noonan syndrome is seen in cardiology clinic for known congenital pulmonary valve stenosis. He is well. His pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 100/62 mmHg. His chest is examined with the stethoscope and the hand.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
o: Continuous machinery murmur below the left clavicle
Crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border with a thrill
Early diastolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge
Pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla
questions.e: Congenital pulmonary stenosis gives a crescendo-decrescendo ejection systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border, often with a palpable thrill.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.
Fixed RV outflow obstruction = **crescendo-decrescendo** ejection murmur in the **pulmonary area**, with a **thrill**.

elim: A machinery murmur is a patent ductus arteriosus.
An early diastolic murmur is pulmonary or aortic regurgitation.
An apical mid-diastolic murmur is mitral stenosis.
An apical pansystolic murmur is mitral regurgitation.

steps.x: **B. Crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border with a thrill.** PS: crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur, left upper sternal border, thrill.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman who grew up in Sudan had rheumatic fever as a child. She has fatigue, abdominal swelling and ankle oedema but little breathlessness. Her JVP is raised at 7 cm. Her liver is enlarged. Her heart is auscultated at the lower left sternal edge.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on auscultation?
o: Early diastolic murmur louder in expiration
Ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids
Pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla
questions.e: Rheumatic tricuspid stenosis gives fatigue, a raised JVP and a mid-diastolic murmur at the lower sternal edge that gets louder with inspiration.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.

clues: fatigue, abdominal swelling and ankle oedema
steps.x: Rheumatic disease + right-sided congestion with little breathlessness = **tricuspid stenosis**: a **diastolic** murmur, louder on **inspiration**.

elim: An early diastolic murmur louder in expiration is aortic regurgitation.
An ejection systolic murmur to the carotids is aortic stenosis.
A pansystolic murmur to the axilla is mitral regurgitation.
A knock is constrictive pericarditis.

steps.x: **C. Mid-diastolic murmur louder on inspiration.** Tricuspid stenosis: mid-diastolic murmur at the lower sternal edge, louder on inspiration.

questions.stem: A 49 year old woman has pulmonary arterial hypertension with an estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure of 78 mmHg. She has a new soft, high-pitched early diastolic murmur at the left upper sternal edge that is louder on inspiration. Her pulse pressure is normal and there is no collapsing pulse.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Pulmonary regurgitation gives an early diastolic murmur and is associated with pulmonary hypertension; louder on inspiration it is right-sided.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.

clues: early diastolic murmur at the left upper sternal edge
steps.x: Early diastolic + **pulmonary hypertension** + louder on **inspiration** + normal pulse pressure = pulmonary regurgitation.

elim: Aortic regurgitation gives a collapsing pulse, a wide pulse pressure and is louder in expiration.
Pulmonary stenosis is an ejection systolic murmur.
Tricuspid stenosis is a mid-diastolic murmur at the lower sternal edge.
A VSD is pansystolic.

steps.x: **B. Pulmonary regurgitation.** Early diastolic murmur with pulmonary hypertension, louder on inspiration: pulmonary regurgitation.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man has heart failure with an ejection fraction of 25% after several myocardial infarctions. He has worsening leg oedema and a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge louder on inspiration. Echocardiography shows structurally normal tricuspid leaflets, a dilated annulus, a dilated right ventricle and a pulmonary artery pressure of 62 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his tricuspid regurgitation?
o: Pulmonary hypertension from left heart failure
questions.e: Left heart failure raises pulmonary pressures; RV afterload rises, the RV dilates and stretches the annulus, giving functional TR with normal leaflets.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.
**Normal leaflets** + **dilated annulus** + high pulmonary pressure from **left HF** = functional (secondary) TR.

elim: Carcinoid thickens and fixes the leaflets.
Endocarditis causes vegetations and leaflet destruction.
Rheumatic disease thickens and fuses the leaflets.
Prolapse is a leaflet abnormality; his leaflets are normal.

steps.x: **C. Pulmonary hypertension from left heart failure.** Most TR is functional, secondary to pulmonary hypertension (often from left heart disease).

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman with systemic sclerosis and pulmonary hypertension has 4 months of fatigue, abdominal swelling and ankle oedema. Her JVP is raised to the earlobes with large waves coinciding with the carotid pulse. There is a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge, a pulsatile liver and shifting dullness.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Tricuspid regurgitation is the most common right-sided valve lesion: systolic backflow gives large CV waves, a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge, pulsatile hepatomegaly and right heart failure.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.

clues: large waves coinciding with the carotid pulse
pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge
steps.x: **Systolic** waves in the JVP + LLSE **pansystolic** murmur + **pulsatile liver** = TR.

elim: MR is heard at the apex radiating to the axilla.
PR gives an early diastolic murmur.
PS gives an ejection systolic murmur in the pulmonary area.
TS gives a diastolic murmur and a large a wave, not a systolic wave.

steps.x: **D. Tricuspid regurgitation.** LLSE pansystolic + V waves + pulsatile liver = tricuspid regurgitation.

questions.stem: A 30 year old man who injects drugs is on day 5 of IV antibiotics for tricuspid valve endocarditis with a large vegetation. He develops sudden sharp right-sided chest pain worse on breathing and coughs up blood-stained sputum. His temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 112 bpm and oxygen saturation 91% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his new symptoms?
questions.e: Tricuspid vegetations embolise into the pulmonary circulation, causing septic pulmonary emboli with pleuritic pain, haemoptysis and hypoxia.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.

clues: tricuspid valve endocarditis with a large vegetation
steps.x: A **right-sided** vegetation can only embolise to the **lungs**: pleuritic pain + haemoptysis = septic PE.

elim: Dissection gives tearing pain and pulse deficits.
Tamponade gives hypotension, raised JVP and muffled sounds.
He is not injecting in hospital and a pneumothorax would not cause haemoptysis and fever.
Right-sided emboli do not reach the brain without a shunt.

steps.x: **D. Septic pulmonary embolism.** Right-sided valve disease complications: right heart failure, pulmonary emboli, arrhythmias.

questions.stem: A 77 year old woman has severe tricuspid regurgitation and a dilated right atrium. She has 1 day of palpitations. Her pulse rate is 150 bpm and regular, BP 118/70 mmHg and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. ECG (see item resources).

visual.title: Rhythm strip
visual.caption: Saw-tooth flutter waves with a regular ventricular rate of 150.

questions.q: Which is the most likely rhythm?
questions.e: A dilated right atrium from tricuspid regurgitation predisposes to arrhythmias; a regular rate of 150 with saw-tooth waves is atrial flutter with 2:1 block, a right atrial macro-reentry.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.
Right atrial dilatation + **regular 150** + saw-tooth waves = **flutter 2:1**.

elim: AF is irregularly irregular.
Sinus tachycardia has normal P waves, not saw-tooth waves.
VT has broad complexes.
WPW shows a short PR and delta wave.

steps.x: **B. Atrial flutter with 2:1 block.** Arrhythmias complicate right heart valve disease; regular 150 = flutter 2:1.

questions.stem: A 9 year old girl has congenital pulmonary valve stenosis found on examination. She has an ejection systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border with a thrill. Her paediatric cardiologist needs to decide whether the stenosis is severe enough to treat.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to assess severity?
questions.e: Echocardiography is the gold standard; Doppler measures the pressure gradient across the pulmonary valve, which grades severity.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or rule out, and when.
Severity of a stenosis = the **pressure gradient**, measured by **echo Doppler**.

elim: MRI is an adjunct, not the first test.
A chest X-ray may show post-stenotic dilatation but cannot grade severity.
An exercise test does not measure the gradient.
BNP does not grade a valve lesion.

steps.x: **C. Echocardiography with Doppler pressure gradient.** Right heart valve disease: echo is the gold standard; Doppler gives the gradient.

questions.stem: A 16 year old boy has moderate pulmonary stenosis with a thickened right ventricle on echocardiography. He is breathless on exertion. His pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 118/70 mmHg. A 12-lead ECG is recorded at his clinic visit.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on the ECG?
o: Delta waves with a short PR interval
Left axis deviation with left bundle branch block
Low-voltage QRS complexes with electrical alternans
Right axis deviation with a dominant R wave in V1
ST elevation in II, III and aVF
questions.e: Pulmonary stenosis causes right ventricular hypertrophy, which shows on the ECG as right axis deviation and a dominant R wave in V1.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or rule out, and when.
RV outflow obstruction thickens the **RV**: ECG shows **right axis deviation** and a tall R in V1.

elim: Delta waves are pre-excitation.
Left axis deviation with LBBB points to left-sided disease.
Electrical alternans is a large pericardial effusion.
Inferior ST elevation is a STEMI.

steps.x: **D. Right axis deviation with a dominant R wave in V1.** ECG and chest X-ray are supporting tests; PS gives right ventricular hypertrophy.

questions.stem: A 79 year old man has long-standing severe tricuspid regurgitation. He has a raised JVP with large systolic waves, pulsatile hepatomegaly and ankle oedema. His pulse rate is 88 bpm and irregular. A chest X-ray is requested.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on chest X-ray?
o: Cardiomegaly with an enlarged right heart border
questions.e: Severe tricuspid regurgitation volume-overloads the right atrium and ventricle, giving cardiomegaly with a prominent right heart border.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or rule out, and when.
Chronic backflow dilates the **right atrium**: an **enlarged right heart border**.

elim: Hilar lymphadenopathy is sarcoid or lymphoma.
A boot-shaped heart is tetralogy of Fallot in children.
Free air is a perforated viscus.
A small calcified heart is constrictive pericarditis.

steps.x: **C. Cardiomegaly with an enlarged right heart border.** TR CXR: cardiomegaly with an enlarged right atrium.

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman had tetralogy of Fallot repaired as a baby. She has increasing breathlessness on exertion. There is a soft early diastolic murmur at the left upper sternal edge, louder on inspiration. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm, BP 116/72 mmHg and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: Echocardiography is the gold standard for right-sided valve disease and will show pulmonary regurgitation, a common late problem after Fallot repair.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or rule out, and when.

clues: early diastolic murmur at the left upper sternal edge
steps.x: Right-sided early diastolic murmur after Fallot repair = **pulmonary regurgitation**; confirm with **echo**.

elim: Catheterisation is invasive and not the first diagnostic test.
A chest X-ray supports but does not confirm valve disease.
CT coronary angiography looks at coronary arteries.
An exercise test assesses capacity, not the valve.

steps.x: **E. Transthoracic echocardiography.** Right heart valve disease: echocardiography is the gold standard.

questions.stem: A 29 year old man who injects drugs has 5 days of fever and rigors. There is a new pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge louder on inspiration. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 114 bpm and BP 116/72 mmHg. He is alert. No antibiotics have been given.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
o: Blood cultures, three sets from different sites
questions.e: Fever, IV drug use and a new murmur suggest right-sided endocarditis, an emergency; three sets of blood cultures before antibiotics identify the organism to treat the underlying infection.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or rule out, and when.
Suspected right-sided **IE**, stable, no antibiotics yet: **three culture sets** first, then treat.

elim: A chest X-ray helps but does not identify the organism.
CTPA looks for thrombotic PE.
Procalcitonin is non-specific.
A drug screen does not change the management of endocarditis.

steps.x: **A. Blood cultures, three sets from different sites.** IVDU + fever + new murmur: three sets of blood cultures, then IV antibiotics.

questions.stem: A 38 year old woman who injects drugs has tricuspid valve endocarditis and new severe tricuspid regurgitation. Three sets of blood cultures have been taken. Her temperature is 38.7°C, pulse rate 108 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. She has mild ankle swelling. Her eGFR is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: IV antibiotics to treat the infection
questions.e: The first principle in right-sided valve disease is treating the underlying cause; here that is the infection, with IV antibiotics.

steps.x: A management question: decide the stage of care and what must happen now.

clues: Three sets of blood cultures have been taken
steps.x: Treat the **cause**: the infection needs **IV antibiotics**. Surgery only for failure or severe uncontrolled disease.

elim: Immediate replacement is not first; antibiotics come first.
Endocarditis needs IV treatment in hospital.
A diuretic treats fluid but not the cause.
Untreated endocarditis is fatal.

steps.x: **B. IV antibiotics to treat the infection.** Right heart valve disease: treat the underlying cause first.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman has rheumatic tricuspid stenosis. She has 3 weeks of increasing abdominal swelling, leg oedema to the knees and a 5 kg weight gain. Her JVP is raised at 9 cm and her liver is enlarged. Her BP is 128/76 mmHg and potassium 4.2 mmol/L. She is awaiting cardiology review.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.e: Diuretics such as furosemide treat fluid overload in right heart valve disease.

steps.x: A management question: decide the stage of care and what must happen now.
She is **fluid overloaded**: start a **loop diuretic**.

elim: Amlodipine causes ankle oedema.
Digoxin is for rate control in AF.
Steroids cause fluid retention.
There is no pericardial effusion.

steps.x: **C. Oral furosemide.** Fluid overload in right heart valve disease: furosemide.

questions.stem: A 55 year old woman has severe rheumatic tricuspid stenosis. Despite high-dose diuretics she has ascites, leg oedema and fatigue that stop her working. Echocardiography confirms a severely narrowed tricuspid valve. She is otherwise fit.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
o: Increase furosemide and review in 1 year
Surgical tricuspid valve repair or replacement
questions.e: Severe symptomatic right heart valve disease is treated definitively with surgical valve repair or replacement.

steps.x: A management question: decide the stage of care and what must happen now.
**Severe**, symptomatic, failing diuretics, fit: **surgery**.

elim: More diuretics have already failed.
The liver congestion is from the valve; transplant does not treat the cause.
Pericardiectomy is for constrictive pericarditis.
Paracentesis relieves ascites but not the cause.

steps.x: **D. Surgical tricuspid valve repair or replacement.** Severe right heart valve disease: surgical repair or replacement.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man has newly diagnosed chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension. Echocardiography shows moderate functional tricuspid regurgitation with structurally normal leaflets. He is in sinus rhythm, has no oedema and his BP is 126/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management of his tricuspid regurgitation?
questions.e: Functional TR comes from pulmonary hypertension dilating the RV and annulus, so first-line management is treating the underlying cause.

steps.x: A management question: decide the stage of care and what must happen now.

clues: functional tricuspid regurgitation with structurally normal leaflets
steps.x: **Functional** TR with **normal leaflets**: the valve is a victim, so treat the **cause**.

elim: Valvuloplasty is for stenosis, not regurgitation.
Surgery is for severe disease; this is moderate and secondary.
There is no infection.
Pericardiectomy is for constriction.

steps.x: **A. Address the underlying pulmonary hypertension.** Functional TR: treat the underlying pulmonary hypertension.

questions.stem: An 81 year old woman with severe tricuspid regurgitation is admitted with worsening right heart failure. She has gross leg oedema, ascites and a raised JVP despite 80 mg oral furosemide daily. She has bowel wall oedema on CT and her BP is 132/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.e: Fluid overload in right heart valve disease is treated with diuretics; bowel oedema reduces oral absorption, so IV furosemide is used.

steps.x: A management question: decide the stage of care and what must happen now.
Oral diuretic is failing because the **gut is oedematous**: give **IV furosemide**.

elim: Fluid restriction alone will not clear this much fluid.
IV saline worsens fluid overload.
A thiazide alone is weaker than her current loop diuretic.
Stopping diuretics would worsen the overload.

steps.x: **B. IV furosemide.** Right heart failure from TR: diuretics, IV if oral absorption fails.

questions.stem: A 32 year old man had tetralogy of Fallot repaired in infancy. He has severe pulmonary regurgitation with a progressively dilating right ventricle on cardiac MRI and reduced exercise capacity. He is otherwise well.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
o: Watch and wait with yearly echo only
questions.e: Severe right-sided valve disease with progressive RV dilatation and symptoms is treated by surgical valve replacement.

steps.x: A management question: decide the stage of care and what must happen now.
**Severe** PR with a **dilating RV** and symptoms: replace the valve before the RV fails.

elim: Valvuloplasty opens stenosis; it would worsen regurgitation.
He is not hypoxic; oxygen does not fix the valve.
Diuretics only treat fluid overload.
Waiting risks irreversible RV failure.

steps.x: **D. Pulmonary valve replacement.** Severe right-sided valve disease: surgical repair or replacement.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman is listed for surgical mitral valve repair for severe degenerative mitral regurgitation. Pre-operative echocardiography also shows severe tricuspid regurgitation with a dilated tricuspid annulus. She has ankle oedema.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management of her tricuspid valve?
o: No treatment, as it will resolve
Tricuspid valve repair at the same operation
questions.e: Severe tricuspid regurgitation is treated with surgical repair, and is repaired at the same time as left-sided valve surgery.

steps.x: A management question: decide the stage of care and what must happen now.

clues: severe tricuspid regurgitation with a dilated tricuspid annulus
steps.x: Severe TR + the chest is already open: **repair it at the same operation**.

elim: Valvuloplasty is for stenosis.
Diuretics alone leave severe TR untreated.
Severe annular dilatation does not reliably resolve after mitral surgery.
A second operation adds avoidable risk.

steps.x: **E. Tricuspid valve repair at the same operation.** Severe TR: surgical repair, ideally with any left-sided surgery.

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman has severe tricuspid regurgitation. Her JVP is raised to 10 cm with a large wave that rises during ventricular systole, at the same time as the carotid pulse, and then falls steeply.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of this wave?
o: Atrial contraction against a closed tricuspid valve
Atrial contraction into a stiff right ventricle
Compression of the heart by pericardial fluid
Obstruction of the superior vena cava
Systolic backflow from the right ventricle into the right atrium
questions.e: In tricuspid regurgitation blood flows back from RV to RA in systole, raising right atrial pressure and producing a prominent V (C-V) wave.

steps.x: A science question: link the finding in the stem to the mechanism behind it.
A wave in **systole** with TR = blood pushed back into the **RA**: giant **CV wave**.

elim: Atrial contraction against a closed valve gives cannon a waves (heart block).
Contraction into a stiff RV gives a large a wave (pulmonary stenosis).
Pericardial compression is tamponade, with an absent y descent.
SVC obstruction gives a raised, non-pulsatile JVP.

steps.x: **E. Systolic backflow from the right ventricle into the right atrium.** TR: systolic backflow raises RA pressure, giving a giant V (CV) wave.

questions.stem: A 73 year old man has had severe tricuspid regurgitation for 10 years. He now has jaundice, a firm irregular liver edge and ascites. He drinks no alcohol and viral hepatitis serology is negative. Liver ultrasound shows dilated hepatic veins and a nodular liver.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his liver disease?
o: Backward transmission of raised venous pressure to the liver
questions.e: Chronic TR raises right atrial and venous pressure, which is transmitted back to the liver, causing pulsatile hepatomegaly, congestion and eventually cardiac cirrhosis.

steps.x: A science question: link the finding in the stem to the mechanism behind it.

clues: dilated hepatic veins and a nodular liver
steps.x: Years of high **venous pressure** congest the liver: **cardiac cirrhosis**.

elim: Primary biliary cholangitis is autoimmune and unrelated to TR.
Haemochromatosis causes iron deposition, not dilated hepatic veins.
Portal vein thrombosis does not dilate the hepatic veins.
Diuretics do not cause cirrhosis.

steps.x: **A. Backward transmission of raised venous pressure to the liver.** Chronic TR: venous congestion of the liver, then cardiac cirrhosis.

questions.stem: A 34 year old man who injects drugs has a tricuspid valve vegetation. CT shows multiple septic emboli in both lungs, but MRI of the brain and CT of the abdomen show no emboli. He has no septal defect on echocardiography.
questions.q: Which best explains this pattern of emboli?
o: Emboli from right-sided vegetations lodge in the lungs
Organisms reach the left heart first in drug users
The blood-brain barrier blocks brain emboli
The spleen filters emboli from the brain
